name: Bai
description: The signature Mizo stew of boiled seasonal vegetables such as spinach, bamboo shoot, string beans and edible ferns with herbs, often flavoured with bekang (fermented soybean) or sa-um (fermented pork). Recipes vary from home to home, and some add pork.
how_to_eat: Eat with steamed rice; some people drink it as a soup first.
how_to_order: Ask for 'bai' at any Mizo eatery in Aizawl; it is found everywhere.

name: Vawksa Rep
description: Smoked pork, cut into cubes and cooked with herbs and often bamboo shoot. It is the most famous Mizo pork dish and a staple at feasts.
how_to_eat: Eat with steamed or sticky rice.
how_to_order: Ask for 'vawksa rep' at Mizo restaurants in Aizawl.

name: Sawhchiar
description: Rice cooked together with beef, pork or chicken into a thick, filling one-pot dish. It is a common Mizo lunch.
how_to_eat: Eat it hot as a full meal.
how_to_order: Ask for 'sawhchiar' and say which meat you want.

name: Arsa Buhchiar
description: A savoury porridge of rice and chicken cooked with ginger, garlic and herbs.
how_to_eat: Eat it hot from a bowl.
how_to_order: Ask for 'arsa buhchiar' at Mizo eateries in Aizawl.

name: Bekang
description: Fermented soybeans, similar to Japanese natto but less slimy, eaten raw or made into a curry with salt, green chillies and tomatoes. A cheap, protein-rich side that matters a lot in Mizo food culture.
how_to_eat: Eat a little with rice and meat.
how_to_order: Ask for 'bekang' at Mizo eateries or buy it at Aizawl markets.

name: Hmarcha Rawt
description: A tangy, spicy chutney of green chillies with garlic and onion, a long-standing staple served with rice.
how_to_eat: Use a little on the side of rice and meat.
how_to_order: Comes with most Mizo meals; ask for 'hmarcha rawt'.

name: Chhum Han
description: Mixed vegetables such as cabbage, beans and leafy greens steamed with ginger and no masala or oil. A light everyday side.
how_to_order: Ask for 'chhum han' with a Mizo meal.
